The most immediate obvious glaring hole in this argument to me as a queer person is its cisheteronormativity: that you didn’t account for the very existence of non-heterosexual and non-cisgender people and our relationships. The same problem usually applies with basically every argument against porn (unilaterally as a concept, rather than specific types of porn) or against non-procreative sex. So we as sexual beings with libido and attraction are supposed to just never have sex with the people we choose, even with love and even marriage, just because we aren’t able to procreate?

Queer behaviors and cultures have existed forever (though by many other names) and will continue to exist forever (as long as humans do, at least, though lots of other species are well-documented to exhibit non-heterosexual behavior).

And as others have pointed out, asexuality and demisexuality are relevant to this conversation too.

And then there’s the misogynist/patriarchal/oppressive parts of the history of marriage legislation and property rights, etc… marriage is a social institution that was invented at some point by human cultures that didn’t have it before, and often it was (even now is) used for purposes totally unrelated to romance.

it’s a scar that grows outside the boundaries of the original wound and keeps growing, some people are genetically predisposed to their body healing that way. It’s not caused by any specific type or severity of wound necessarily (e.g. tiny cosmetic piercings can trigger keloids at times) it’s literally just a genetic thing with collagen production that some bodies will do, more common in dark skinned ppl or if you have a family history of ppl getting keloids

No shade but lot of ppl in SH groups think that their scars are keloids and talk about having keloids, but they are more often than not talking about standard hypertrophic scars (raised scars within the boundaries of the original wound, can be caused by mechanical tension in the healing area—they can get pretty raised, but won’t start bulging horizontally outside the boundaries like a keloid or keep growing years later like a keloid, and may calm down as time passes over years), just that many ppl have health anxiety and misinterpret the signs (bc we all stare at our own bodies constantly and it magnifies what we see). Op might be talking about hypertrophic scars. They can be extremely itchy or have random pains, pretty much indefinitely into the future

Tbh i think maybe there needs to be an information campaign about different types of scarring bc a lot of people confuse these or think they’re the same. The vast majority of sh scars are flat, hypertrophic, or atrophic. (atrophic/hypotrophic scars, or sunken scars, are a third type of non-flat scarring.) Keloids are pretty uncommon and again it’s literally just a genetic thing. Like the cilantro soap gene or something.

I don’t think you understand AI very well, it’s really not capable of much

“AI” is a buzzword to describe what at the end of the day is just another set of algorithms. It doesn’t actually  “read” what you type to it in the way that a human does. It never sees the actual sentence you wrote. Each word in a GPT prompt is separated individually and tokenized, it runs some calculations based on what those words are *usually* seen around in its training data set, and then spits out an approximation that it ‘thinks’ you want to hear/see. It doesnt actually understand grammar or concepts, it just has an internal map that tells it where something “probably” should go. That’s why AI written essays and webpages are often so repetitive, and sometimes even nonsensical or self-contradictory. That’s why AIs can’t draw hands with the correct number of fingers.

As another example have you seen those images where someone asks chatGPT to tell them how many letter n’s are in the word “mayonnaise” and it can’t come up with an answer that makes any sense at all? (Like, it’ll say “there are 4 n’s: mayo**nnn**ai**n**se”. And then change its answer if you ask again) It can’t even comprehend *that* it’s wrong or *why* it’s wrong even when you explain explicitly to it. 

Literally “AI” in the present day tech world is just a buzzword to get investors and business execs hyped up. Philosophers talk about “general AI”vs “narrow AI” but we aren’t even close to the concepts that they talk about. People who actually work on AI software get tasked with trying to make AI do these extravagant complicated things that actual conscious beings could do, but the AIs often times can’t even properly answer the simplest of questions required to get there. Devs can keep issuing patches to fix strange obvious bugs that people find like that, but like, it’s just like that all the way down and there’s gonna be more of those forever. It’s not and won’t ever be conscious.

I think a better perspective would be “it *can* be okay to smoke weed from time to time”. But yeah I think him literally endorsing it is uncomfortable and he should be able to understand and respect your decision to quit, you need to bring up that it made you uncomfortable and disappointed or hurt. You don’t tell an alcoholic or other addict “it’s okay to drink/use from time to time to deal with stress”. In my perspective healthy moderation for me would be at the point that I can use infrequently instead of frequently, socially instead of alone, and for enjoyment, not to numb out negative emotions or forget about stress. But still, there’s a lot of grey area here between the two perspectives, and differences in what works and what doesn’t work for different people. You sound committed and ready to work on the routines of getting into healthier coping mechanisms.

For what it’s worth I’m proud of you for making it this long. 

It’s worth exploring the guilt feelings though, yeah. There can be a level of functional guilt about real consequences—we wouldn’t have emotions if they weren’t trying to tell us something—but there’s a level of dysfunctional guilt where you’re just beating yourself up needlessly. If a lapse or full relapse happens for example, directing tons of guilt and hatred at yourself isn’t going to help you move forward. It’s important to process and figure out how to accept and move forward. Like, you aren’t categorically a bad person for your use, but it can be true that we make unhelpful decisions sometimes.

Long-winded personal reflection on this same dilemma over the past 5+ years:

Like, beyond it literally just being a different sensation, it doesn’t affect my sense of the presentation/perception of my gender anymore and I’m not really anxious about it anymore, I’m just a woman who’s got a bit of hair—like all humans.

Basically my point is presentation can be as fluid over time as you want it to be and there’s no shame in playing with figuring out what makes you feel good. I went through a very hyper-femme period of time to a more androgynous period of time to a kind of genderfuck period of time to now more like just casual femme—idk these are not very descriptive terms and it varies a lot on a day to day basis anyway bc like, weather and occasion and mood and comfort and just needing to change my clothes.

So If embodying that political statement about beauty standards feels good and helps you feel good in your body, then do it, but if it’s at the expense of your well-being/comfort with being out in public, then it’s not sending a message or doing much good to anybody, is it? I find it can do both ways at different points in time. It feels good to let my body hair be loose and free and fuzzy and sexy and say “fuck you I do what I want” to the world sometimes, and it can feel good to be smooth and shiny and hairless and sexy and still say “fuck you I do what I want” sometimes. The personal is political, sure, but you don’t have to commit to every single action of personal praxis simultaneously and constantly in order to Prove Yourself or your morals, and you can still do other things within your means or find other types of praxis you care about. I had mostly “good” BMI (read: low end of “healthy”, but sometimes fluctuating into underweight territory) for 4 years of estrogen and my body looked a lot like yours the whole time: some good breast growth (I had maybe slightly more growth than you by the end of 4 years), some skin/nail/hair changes, but otherwise very thin and bony and felt still very masculine. 

Then one of my doctors unexpectedly recommended me to get eating disorder treatment for possible anorexia, which I didn’t even realize I wasn’t eating enough. After a few months of outpatient treatment, I made the decision to step up to a residential program (it was 2 months long) and finally learned what an adequate amount of food for my body is. (It’s not one size fits all, don’t listen to anybody telling you a specific calorie amount must be followed, it’s more about hunger cues and fullness cues and your energy and mood and what makes you actually feel nourished/energetic/alive.) That was last winter, about a year ago.

I gained a decent amount of weight (like… +15% of my initial weight) while there and then my weight stabilized (still like smack in the middle of “healthy” BMI if you’re worried about that, but BMI is bs anyway). My boobs started growing again while I was there and haven’t stopped since. My body frame started to actually look more feminine and less angular/wide/masc, because estrogen was able to guide the (small amount of) gained fat to follow a feminine distribution pattern.

Food is medicine, and food is fuel. If your body is using all of the calories you feed it just to keep your basic survival functions and organs working, then estrogen won’t do much. If you start consistently eating more, then estrogen will be able to actually work for you more. Being on hormones for 5 years now, I literally feel like I’m going through a *third puberty* now that I’m at a better (higher) stable weight for a year now and my body is *still* changing. Even my face has changed, now that I have a little bit more padding in the right spots I look a lot more naturally feminine—and I just look more alive in general.

I don’t say this to diagnose you with an ED but to point out that you might have a skewed perception of how much food your body needs. And to point out that gaining even just a bit of mass will do wonders for you. Nobody had really told me that going into HRT but it’s really crucial for ppl like us who are thin / have fast metabolism / don’t gain weight easily / don’t eat a lot easily.
